symptoms: Small (under 3mm) dark brown to black circular lesions on leaves, often water-soaked initially
Yellow chlorotic halos surround spots, giving a speckled appearance
Leaf lesions may coalesce leading to ragged leaf margins and scorched appearance
Fruit exhibits raised, scab-like, blistered spots with dark margins
management: Avoid entering or handling crops while foliage is wet from rain or dew to prevent bacterial spreading.
Carefully remove badly affected leaves or seedlings; disinfect pruning shears with 70% alcohol or 10% bleach between plants.
Do not rely solely on routine copper sprays; copper-resistant Xanthomonas strains are widespread in commercial tomato basins in Kenya.
prevention: Source hot-water treated or certified disease-free commercial seeds from reputable seed houses.
Use drip irrigation under mulch rather than overhead sprinklers to eliminate water splash.
Practice strict 2-3 year crop rotation away from solanaceous crops (tomato, pepper, potato, black nightshade).
Ensure adequate plant spacing and staking/trellising for rapid drying.
monitoring: Scout nursery seedbeds and newly transplanted crops closely after warm thunderstorms.
Check young tender foliage and developing green fruit for water-soaked greasy spots.
escalation: Spotting observed in seedling nursery prior to transplanting (do not transplant infected seedlings).
Rapid spread after overhead irrigation or hail damage with fruit lesions appearing.
Extensive defoliation exposing green fruit to sunscald.
kenya_notes: Very common in warm humid tomato growing belts including Kirinyaga (Mwea irrigation scheme), Machakos, Kajiado, and lakeside regions. Overhead irrigation substantially amplifies outbreaks.
